newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU to meet unions, employers on code of conduct.
newsitem.headline: EU to meet unions, employers on code of conduct.

text.p: Dutch Employment Minister Ad Melkert said on Monday he would meet trade unionists and employers on April 15 in Brussels to discuss a code of conduct for companies planning plant closures.

The move was prompted by French car giant Renault, which shocked workers in late February with an announcement that it would close its profitable Vilvoorde plant in Belgium with the loss of 3,100 jobs.
Melkert announced the move to a group of Europe's top companies, telling them it was critical for them to involve workers in their major decisions.

Melkert, whose country holds the European Union presidency, used the occasion of a luncheon sponsored by European Round Table of Industrialists (ERT) to make a plea for a "social partnership" between employers and workers.

"Job creation and job cancellation are daily practice in a modern, open European economy," Melkert told the ERT, which launched a new study calling for closer cooperation between big and small companies to boost Europe's competitiveness.
"But this does not mean that these are autonomous processes. They cannot be detached from their social context."
Melkert was joined by EU Social Affairs Commissioner Padraig Flynn, who told the group:
"The Renault case shows that we still have some way to go to strike the right balance between corporate needs and those of workers and society as a whole."
The April 15 meeting, which will also involve the European Commission, has been scheduled as a follow-up to an informal meeting of EU social affairs ministers in Rotterdam last month.
The ministers called for a clear code of conduct governing business closures, which should ensure a period of consultation and information.
They also suggested governments should strengthen their national laws to avoid a repeat of the Renault scenario.

Vilvoorde's angry Renault workers won moral victories in Belgium and France last week when courts ruled Renault had broken the law on prior consultation with workers and therefore had to restart the closure process from scratch.
However Renault said this did not affect its plan to close the plant.

Morris Tabaksblat, chairman and CEO of Unilever, who presented the ERT's new report, declined to comment on Renault's "tactics" but said it was wrong to assume that plant restructurings were always "anti-social".
Sometimes, he said, "You're totally anti-social if you don't do it because the effect in the long-term is much worse than if you face it head on."
He noted that Renault had been involved in a case study included in the new ERT report, cited for launching a programme for training unqualified secondary school leavers.
